the macroalgae were opportunistic and that the source of the N supporting their growth was initially fertilizer-derived.

opportunistic green macroalgal growth was supported by N from fertilizers in agricultural soil during the first year after flooding, whereas inorganic N was depleted by the second year as a result of dilution and flushing by seawater.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the first year of flooding is a critical period for macroalgal blooms in managed realignment projects, but that the nutrient status will rapidly change as the ecosystem develops.
managed realignment may risk enrichment of coastal waters with N from agricultural land but that the risk is reduced over time due to dilution by seawater and nutrient depletion.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the isotopic signature of opportunistic macroalgaea can be used as a proxy to identify the origin of N in the early phase of managed realignment, which is of importance for future coastal management.
opportunistic green macroalgal growth is likely to be a short-term phenomenon in newly flooded areas and will be replaced by more permanent macroalgal species as the ecosystem matures.

opportunistic macroalgaea can be a useful bioindicator of the origin of N in coastal waters, and the isotopic composition can be used to monitor the effects of land use and land management on coastal waters.
